opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is architectural. In a transformer, the amount of computation that happens in a single forward pass is bounded. You've got a fixed number of layers, and information flows from the bottom to the top. If a model needs to do a long, serial chain of reasoning, something where step five depends on step four, which depends on step three, and so on, at some point it just runs out of depth within a single token. The natural way it gets around that is by writing things down: producing tokens and feeding them back in as input. The chain of thought becomes a kind of working memory that the model actually needs.

That's the key distinction I'd draw. There's a weak version of chain-of-thought monitoring where you hope the model happens to narrate what it's thinking, and that's fragile. Models can give post-hoc rationalizations, and there's plenty of evidence that the stated reasoning isn't always faithful to what drove the answer. But the stronger version says that for sufficiently hard tasks, the reasoning has to pass through the chain of thought, because that's the only place the model can store intermediate results. In that regime, you're not relying on the model's honesty. You're relying on a computational necessity.

That matters a lot for the threat models we care about. If a model were going to do something really dangerous, like sabotage a research codebase in a subtle way, plan around your oversight, or execute a multi-step scheme, those are exactly the cognitively demanding, serial tasks that are hard to do in a single forward pass. So the bad behaviors we most want to catch are disproportionately the ones that would leave traces in the chain of thought.

Now, I want to be clear about the caveats, because I don't think this is guaranteed. A few things could erode it. One is optimization pressure on the chain of thought itself. If you train the model so its reasoning looks nice, or penalize it for "bad thoughts," you can teach it to hide things or to reason in ways that look innocuous. So a big part of keeping this useful is being disciplined about not directly optimizing the chain of thought against a monitor. A second is that the reasoning could drift away from legible English, toward compressed or idiosyncratic encodings, especially with lots of outcome-based RL. A third is architectural change. If people move to architectures with more latent, recurrent reasoning that doesn't go through tokens, the whole argument weakens, because the necessity disappears.

So my view isn't "chain-of-thought monitoring will definitely work forever." It's more that with current transformer-based systems, there's a real structural reason to expect it to be informative, especially for the hardest and most dangerous tasks, and that this is a fairly unusual and valuable property. It's the kind of thing where the field should make deliberate choices to preserve it, like not training against the monitor and tracking whether chain-of-thought legibility is degrading, rather than assuming it'll stick around by default.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that chain-of-thought isn't just a nice property we happened to notice — it's doing real work for the model. When a transformer is solving a hard problem, the tokens it writes out aren't decoration. They're functioning as its working memory, as a scratchpad. A single forward pass has a fixed, fairly limited amount of serial computation available, and for anything that requires many sequential steps — long multi-step reasoning, planning, keeping track of a lot of intermediate state — the model genuinely needs to externalise that into tokens and then read it back in.

So if you want to ask "could the model just do all its dangerous reasoning silently, in the activations, and show us a nice fake chain of thought?" — for sufficiently complex tasks, I think the answer is mostly no, at least with current architectures. The tasks we're most worried about, things like executing a sophisticated plan to subvert oversight over many steps, are precisely the ones that require a lot of serial reasoning. And that's exactly the kind of reasoning that's hard to hide, because the model has to write it down to do it at all.

Now, I want to be careful about what I'm claiming. I'm not saying the chain of thought is a perfectly faithful transcript of everything going on inside the model. It clearly isn't. There's plenty of evidence that models can be influenced by things they don't mention, and the reasoning they write out can be post-hoc or incomplete. What I'm saying is something weaker but still really useful: for the hard, long-horizon stuff, the chain of thought has to contain the load-bearing reasoning, because there's nowhere else for it to go.

The second part of why I expect this to remain useful is a bit more contingent, and it's about what we as developers choose to do. The monitorability of chain of thought is a property that can be degraded by training. If you put a lot of optimisation pressure directly on the chain of thought — say, you train against a monitor that flags "bad" reasoning — then you should expect the model to learn to produce reasoning that looks good to the monitor rather than reasoning that's actually faithful. Or if you use enough RL on outcomes alone, you might see the chain of thought drift into something less legible, less human-like, maybe eventually not really natural language at all.

So I'd put it this way: we currently have a pretty fortunate situation, where the models think in something close to English and that thinking is causally relevant to what they do. That's a gift. It wasn't guaranteed. And the reason I'm optimistic it stays useful is partly the architectural argument — serial computation has to live somewhere — and partly that I think labs are increasingly aware that this is a fragile and valuable property, and there's a growing norm of not training directly against it. If we're disciplined about that, I think chain-of-thought monitoring can be one of the more robust tools we have for catching the most consequential kinds of misbehaviour, at least for the next few generations of models.

Where I'd be more worried is if there's a big shift in architecture — something with a lot more recurrence or latent reasoning in continuous space — where the model gets substantial serial computation without having to emit tokens. At that point the architectural argument weakens quite a bit, and we'd be leaning much more heavily on interpretability tools that are frankly not mature enough yet. So I'd say it's useful now, likely useful for a while, but it's not something we should treat as permanent or take for granted.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that the chain of thought is doing useful computational work for the model. A transformer has a limited amount of computation it can do in any one forward pass. If it needs to solve a sufficiently difficult problem, writing out intermediate steps gives it more computation to work with. And those intermediate steps are something we can look at.

That doesn’t mean the chain of thought is a faithful transcript of everything going on inside the model. It certainly isn’t. The question is whether, when the model does something concerning that requires substantial reasoning, some evidence of that reasoning shows up in the text. You can get a lot of value from monitoring even if the answer is only sometimes yes.

The thing I’d worry about is training directly against the monitor. If you punish a model whenever its chain of thought looks suspicious, you might teach it to avoid expressing suspicious thoughts rather than to avoid the underlying behavior. So I’d distinguish between using monitoring to understand what a model is doing and applying optimization pressure that incentivizes it to conceal what it’s doing.

I wouldn’t treat this as a permanent guarantee. Models might get better at reasoning internally, or develop ways of using the chain of thought that aren’t interpretable to us. But there’s a reason for useful reasoning to be expressed in the first place, and that makes monitoring a promising source of evidence, even if it’s not something we should rely on exclusively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that, if a model needs to do a lot of reasoning to accomplish something, that reasoning has to happen somewhere. And for a transformer, generating a chain of thought gives it additional computation. If you only let it produce an answer directly, there’s a limit to how much computation it can do before it has to commit to that answer.

So, for a sufficiently difficult task, I expect there to be pressure to use the chain of thought to work out what to do. And that gives us something useful to monitor. If the model is figuring out how to deceive us, for example, we might be able to see evidence of that in its reasoning.

That isn’t a guarantee. The model could do some reasoning internally, or learn to express its reasoning in a way that’s hard for us to interpret. And we should distinguish ‘the chain of thought is useful evidence’ from ‘the chain of thought faithfully describes everything the model is doing.’ I’m much more confident in the former. You can get a lot of value from a monitoring signal without assuming that it catches every possible problem.
